title: Irenaeus against contempt for matter
hookLine: against those who called the world evil, he defended bodies and creation

cards: An aching back. Bad news on the phone. Someone you love, sick.
For some teachers in the early church, there was a tidy explanation for all of it: the world itself was the mistake. Matter was a trap, built by a lesser power, and the body was a cage.
Salvation meant secret knowledge, and the secret was how to get out. Later writers group these teachers under the name Gnostic, though they did not all agree.
A bishop in Lyon, in Gaul, thought they had it exactly backward. His name was Irenaeus, and he wrote a long work called Against Heresies.

teach.b: Irenaeus starts where the Bible starts. Genesis closes the sixth day with a verdict: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." Not a mistake.
Very good. Rocks, rivers, animals, bodies.
Then he points to the center of the faith: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." If flesh were a cage, why would God's own Word step into it? Then the table.
Bread comes from the earth and wine from the vine, and in the Eucharist, he argues, these ordinary things receive the word of God and become the gift of Christ's body and blood.

If wheat and grapes can carry that, how can anyone say the flesh is worthless? And forward, to the resurrection. The Apostles' Creed confesses the resurrection of the body: not a soul set loose, but a body raised.
For Irenaeus, the whole story is God making, and then God mending what was made, not God throwing it away.

teach.h: THE GLORY OF GOD, FULLY ALIVE.
teach.b: He sums it up in a line, here in paraphrase: the glory of God is a human being fully alive, and human life is seeing God.
Paul says something close: "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?" A temple, not a cage.
Some churches draw on this when they care for the sick, bless fields and gardens, and bury their dead with care. Bodies matter. Bread matters.
The ground under your feet matters.

how: Christians confess God as maker of heaven and earth and the resurrection of the body in their creeds; churches honor the body through sacraments that use water, bread, wine and oil, through care for the sick, and through Christian burial.

games.q: what does “irenaeus against contempt for matter” mean?
o: a bishop defending the body and creation as good
a monk's warning to scorn every bodily comfort
a scientist's case against the idea of atoms

p: ordinary things that carry a gift

s: Irenaeus taught that the body is a prison the soul should escape
that's the idea he argued against. he defended bodies and creation as God's good work.
Genesis says God saw every thing he had made, and it was very good
Irenaeus pointed to the bread and wine of the Eucharist in defending the body
if bread from the earth and wine from the vine can carry God's gift, he argued, the flesh is not worthless.

games.q: you're a bishop in Lyon. teachers in your city say the world is a mistake and the body is a cage. what do you do?
o: write back: God made the world good, and the Word became flesh.
games.why: Irenaeus wrote a long work against them, pointing to creation, the Word made flesh, the bread and wine, and the resurrection of the body.

practice: Start at your feet and move slowly up, legs, back, hands, shoulders, face, noticing without judging where you're tired and where you're carrying something.
Then pick one small act of care for today: a glass of water, a walk around the block, an early night. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body, the one Genesis would call very good.

wordCard.voice: Irenaeus against contempt for matter. A bishop defending creation and the body as God's good work, against teachers who called the world a trap.

orig.note: Latin, Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.20.7: the glory of God is a living human being.

carryVoice: Your line: matter matters. A temple, not a cage. Same time tomorrow.
